questions.statement:
The European Island That Swaps Nationality Twice a Year
Sophie-May Williams
01
“There are no pheasants __ Pheasant Island,” complained the French author Victor Hugo
02 __ 1843. Calm down, Mr. Hugo. The lack __ game birds is the least interesting thing __ the
03 place. Less than 200 meters long and 40 meters wide, this tiny stretch of land on the Bidasoa
04 River between France and Spain boasts something truly unique: it changes nationality every six
05 months.
06
Let’s backtrack a bit. Pheasant Island is uninhabited, briefly home to migratory birds and
07 wild animals, and lush with greenery. Sunshine is permanent, thanks to the year-long subtropical
08 climate. The only structure is a 19th-century monolith that shares both Spanish and French
09 inscriptions, a symbol of peace between the two nations. But there’s more to this geopolitical
10 anomaly than meets the eye. From February 1 to July 31, it’s under Spanish rule. Then, from
11 August 1 to January 31, it belongs to France.
12
Despite adhering to such a curious concept, few people have heard of the island. Or what
13 it stands for. Back in 1659, it served as the signing location for the Treaty of the Pyrenees. This
14 was a significant peace treaty between Louis XIV of France and Philip IV of Spain, as it ended
15 the 30-year Franco-Spanish War. Remember the tomb-like monolith from earlier? It was erected
16 centuries later to commemorate this very meeting. In simple terms, it gave each nation the
17 chance to govern the humanless island. Sharing is caring, after all. The occasion was so
18 momentous that a year later, French King Louis XIV married the daughter of King Philip IV, Maria
19 Theresa of Spain, in the exact spot where the treaty was signed. Wooden bridges were erected
20 so royal entourages could pass through in barges and carriages, and paintings were
21 commissioned to immortalize the event.
22
These days, general access to Pheasant Island is prohibited. The only time you might be
23 able to set

Which verb tense is mainly used throughout the second paragraph, and why is it used?

options.text: Simple present, because it describes facts about the island — things that will probably not change in the near future.
Present perfect, because the present facts described are consequences of actions that happened in the past.
Simple past, because the past events have a clear time reference.
Simple present, because the events described are not permanent, but temporary.
Present perfect, because the stated events do not have a past time reference.

questions.explanation: O simple present descreve fatos, características e estados habituais ou relativamente estáveis da ilha. O present perfect liga passado e presente, enquanto o simple past situa fatos concluídos; não se trata de acontecimentos apenas temporários.

questions.statement:
The Benefits of Board Games for Students
01
Board games challenge students to think critically, weigh their options, and adapt strategies
02 in real time. Unlike passive learning, games like Rush Hour require active decision-making where
03 each move has consequences. When ____ (calculate) risks in Chess or ____ (predict) an
04 opponent’s next move in Onitama, students strengthen skills such as strategic planning, logical
05 reasoning, and problem-solving. These abilities not only enhance academic performance but also
06 prepare them for real-world challenges requiring quick thinking and adaptability.
07
Many games also reinforce academic skills in a fun, low-pressure way. Unlike traditional
08 worksheets or drills, games like Codenames, Sushi Go Party!, and Letter Tycoon provide
09 hands-on learning experiences that encourage students to think critically. Whether they are
10 calculating scores, forming words, or recognizing patterns, students absorb key math and literacy
11 concepts. Because board games naturally reward effort and strategy, they help students build
12 confidence in these areas, making them more likely to approach academic challenges with a
13 positive mindset.
14
Losing a game can be frustrating, but it also presents a valuable lesson in resilience and
15 emotional regulation. Options like Sorry!, Forbidden Island, and Karuba help students develop a
16 growth mindset, teaching them how to handle setbacks, adapt strategies, and persist through
17 challenges. These experiences translate directly into better emotional resilience in school and
18 everyday life.
19
With constant digital distractions, sustained attention has become a valuable skill. Board
20 games nurture focus by requiring players to plan ahead and remain attentive throughout the
21 game. Unlike fast-paced video games that often shorten attention spans, board games reward
22 concentration and patience. For students with attention challenges, games like Go (Baduk) can
23 be particularly

Mark the alternative that fills in, correctly and respectively, the blanks in the first paragraph.
questions.explanation: Após “When”, o texto usa orações reduzidas de valor temporal: “calculating risks” e “predicting an opponent’s next move”. As formas em -ing mantêm paralelismo e exprimem ações em curso; infinitivos, formas finitas e futuros não se ajustam à construção.

A One-Man Recycling Revolution on The Cornish Coast
By Rupert Neate
01
Ian Falconer kept thinking ___ the heaps of discarded plastic fishing nets he saw at Newlyn
02 harbour near his home ___ Cornwall, England. Falconer, 52, who studied environmental and
03 mining geology ___ university, came up with a plan: shredding and cleaning the worn-out nets,
04 melting the plastic down, and converting it ___ filament to be used in 3D printing. He then built
05 a “micro-factory” so that the filament could be made into useful stuff. “Every year, up to 1 million
06 tonnes of fishing nets are discarded,” he says. “Most of that ends up in landfill or is burned, or
07 worse still, finds its way back into the oceans. This showed there was another way for some of
08 that material”.
09
The first big challenge he encountered when he started in 2016 was getting hold of the nets.
10 But he badgered the Newlyn harbour master into giving him a few to test his theory in his kitchen.
11 Since its launch the following year, Falconer’s company OrCA has raised more than £1m from
12 small investors in over 40 countries. The investment funded the development of patented new
13 machinery that can convert more than 20 kilos of nylon fishing nets an hour. He claims the
14 recycling process has less than 3% of the carbon impact of producing new nylon.

19 the raw material: sunglasses, light shades, bottle openers, razor blade handles. It can be used

questions.statement:
The secret history of Stonehenge
By James Owens
01
Stonehenge, located in southern England, ranks among the world’s most iconic
02 archaeological sites and one of its greatest enigmas. The megalithic stone circle on Salisbury
03 Plain inspires awe and fascination — but also intense debate some 4,600 years after it was built
04 by ancient Britons who left no written record.
05
The monument’s mysterious past has spawned countless tales and theories. According to
06 folklore, Stonehenge was created ___ Merlin, the wizard of Arthurian legend, who magically
07 transported the massive stones ___ Ireland, where giants had assembled them.
08
Another legend says invading Danes put the stones up, and another theory says they were
09 the ruins of a Roman temple. Modern-day interpretations are no less colorful. Some argue that
10 Stonehenge is a spacecraft landing area for aliens, and even more say it’s a giant fertility symbol
11 in the shape of female genitalia.
12
Archaeological investigation of the site dates back to the 1660s, when it was first surveyed
13 by antiquarian John Aubrey. He wrongly credited Stonehenge to the much later Celts, believing
14 it to be a religious center presided over by Druid priests.
15
Centuries of fieldwork since show the Neolithic monument, now a UNESCO World Heritage
16 site, was more than a millennium in the making. It started out 5,000 years ago as a circular
17 earthen bank and ditch, in a larger area of burial mounds.
18
Modern debate over the monument’s meaning has two main camps: those who see it as a
19 holy site, and others who believe it represents a scientific observatory.
20

21 the sun and moon as evidence of rituals linked to the changing seasons and

01
Harvesting solar energy in orbit and beaming it down to Earth is a decades-old idea. Now,
02 a growing number of companies say they could finally make it a reality.
03
At an American football stadium in Florida last March, an unusual test took place. It wasn’t
04 footballs being thrown, but beams of light fired across the length of the pitch. The concentrated
05 streaks of light lasted for a few minutes, sent from an emitter on one side of the Jacksonville
06 Jaguars’ stadium and collected on a screen on the other.
07
The light had been collected from the Sun and then beamed out by large lenses on the field,
08 each about 1.2 metres (4ft) tall, acting like magnifying glasses. “We had to get up a ladder to
09 pull the cover off”, said Andrew Rush, chief executive of the Florida-based company Star Catcher,
10 which carried out the test. “We beamed 100 watts about 105 metres”.
11
The goal was simple: to see if sunlight could be beamed across space to power satellites or
12 even cities on Earth.
13
Space-based solar power aims to capture sunlight in orbit and _____________ it to the
14 ground as clean, renewable energy. Solar panels on Earth are limited by the atmosphere, the
15 weather and the day-night cycle. But in space, sunlight can be collected almost constantly, at
16 much higher ___________.
17
He recalled telling his father about the idea, who thought it sounded rather unrealistic. Yet,
18 as engineer David Homfray explained, “Space-based solar power makes the energy transition
19 work”. Some estimates suggest it could one day provide up to 80% of Europe’s renewable energy
20 needs.
21
Still, making it work is no small task. It would require enormous satellite structures,
22 complex operations and countless rocket launches. And there are cheaper renewable solutions
23 that could come online far faster — a crucial point if the world is to replace fossil fuels in time to
24 limit global warming.

questions.statement:
The Century-Long Search for the Loch* Ness Monster
01
For almost a hundred years, people around the world have been fascinated by the mystery
02 of the Loch Ness Monster, often called “Nessie”. The story began in 1933, when a local couple
03 reported seeing a large creature moving through the dark waters of Loch Ness in the Scottish
04 Highlands. Since then, hundreds of alleged sightings have been recorded.
05
In the 1930s, the legend grew after a photograph published in a newspaper appeared to
06 show a long-necked animal rising from the water. Decades later, the picture was revealed to be
07 a hoax — a small model made with a toy submarine. Still, the myth continued to capture people’s
08 imagination.
09
Over the years, scientists and researchers have tried to find evidence of the monster’s
10 existence. In the 1960s and 1970s, several expeditions used sonar equipment to scan the depths
11 of the loch, detecting some unexplained movements. More recently, drones and underwater
12 cameras have been used to search for signs of life beneath the surface.
13
In 2019, a team from New Zealand analyzed the DNA present in the water and found no
14 trace of any giant reptile or mysterious creature. However, they did find large amounts of eel*
15 DNA, suggesting that the famous monster could actually be a giant eel.
16
Despite the lack of proof, many visitors continue to travel to Scotland hoping to catch a
17 glimpse of Nessie. Whether it is a scientific mystery or just a legend, the Loch Ness Monster
18 remains one of the world’s most famous and enduring myths.
(Available at: www.bbc.com/culture/article/20251002-the-century-long-search-for-the-loch-ness-monster – text specially adapted for this test).
*Loch: in Scotland, a lake or inlet of the sea or ocean. (Available at: https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-portuguese/loch)
*Eel: a snake-like water creature. (Available at: https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-portuguese/eel)

Based on the excerpt below, taken from the text, analyze the following statements: “In 2019, a team from New Zealand analyzed the DNA present in the water and found no trace of any giant reptile or mysterious creature”. I. The verbs “analyzed” and “found” are both in the simple past tense, expressing completed actions. II. The word “any” emphasizes the absence of something. III. The sentence refers to an investigation that started in the past and is still in progress. Which ones are correct?
questions.explanation: 'Analyzed' e 'found' estão no simple past e indicam ações concluídas em 2019. Em construção negativa, 'any' reforça a ausência de vestígio. Nada na frase indica investigação ainda em andamento, leitura que exigiria outra construção verbal ou contexto.

By James Owens
01
Stonehenge, located in southern England, ranks among the world’s most iconic
02 archaeological sites and one of its greatest enigmas. The megalithic stone circle on Salisbury
03 Plain inspires awe and fascination — but also intense debate some 4,600 years after it was built
04 by ancient Britons who left no written record.
05
The monument’s mysterious past has spawned countless tales and theories. According to
06 folklore, Stonehenge was created ___ Merlin, the wizard of Arthurian legend, who magically
07 transported the massive stones ___ Ireland, where giants had assembled them.
08
Another legend says invading Danes put the stones up, and another theory says they were
09 the ruins of a Roman temple. Modern-day interpretations are no less colorful. Some argue that
10 Stonehenge is a spacecraft landing area for aliens, and even more say it’s a giant fertility symbol
11 in the shape of female genitalia.
12
Archaeological investigation of the site dates back to the 1660s, when it was first surveyed
13 by antiquarian John Aubrey. He wrongly credited Stonehenge to the much later Celts, believing
14 it to be a religious center presided over by Druid priests.
15
Centuries of fieldwork since show the Neolithic monument, now a UNESCO World Heritage
16 site, was more than a millennium in the making. It started out 5,000 years ago as a circular
17 earthen bank and ditch, in a larger area of burial mounds.
18
Modern debate over the monument’s meaning has two main camps: those who see it as a
19 holy site, and others who believe it represents a scientific observatory.
20
Both camps base their theories on the site’s celestial influence. They point to alignments to
21 the sun and moon as evidence of rituals linked to the changing seasons and
22 the summer and winter solstices.
23

Analyze the following statements about the words “The megalithic stone” (l. 02): I. The article “the” is correct because it specifies a particular noun. II. It would be grammatically correct to use “an” as a non-specific article because of the pronunciation rule. III. It would be grammatically correct to use “a” as a non-specific article because of the pronunciation rule. Which ones are correct?
questions.explanation: 'The' individualiza o grupo nominal no contexto. Se a referência fosse indefinida, caberia 'a megalithic stone', porque 'megalithic' começa com som consonantal /m/. 'An' exigiria som vocálico inicial, portanto essa afirmação está incorreta.

questions.statement:
Space power: The dream of beaming solar energy from orbit
01
Harvesting solar energy in orbit and beaming it down to Earth is a decades-old idea. Now,
02 a growing number of companies say they could finally make it a reality.
03
At an American football stadium in Florida last March, an unusual test took place. It wasn’t
04 footballs being thrown, but beams of light fired across the length of the pitch. The concentrated
05 streaks of light lasted for a few minutes, sent from an emitter on one side of the Jacksonville
06 Jaguars’ stadium and collected on a screen on the other.
07
The light had been collected from the Sun and then beamed out by large lenses on the field,
08 each about 1.2 metres (4ft) tall, acting like magnifying glasses. “We had to get up a ladder to
09 pull the cover off”, said Andrew Rush, chief executive of the Florida-based company Star Catcher,
10 which carried out the test. “We beamed 100 watts about 105 metres”.
11
The goal was simple: to see if sunlight could be beamed across space to power satellites or
12 even cities on Earth.
13
Space-based solar power aims to capture sunlight in orbit and _____________ it to the
14 ground as clean, renewable energy. Solar panels on Earth are limited by the atmosphere, the
15 weather and the day-night cycle. But in space, sunlight can be collected almost constantly, at
16 much higher ___________.
17
He recalled telling his father about the idea, who thought it sounded rather unrealistic. Yet,
18 as engineer David Homfray explained, “Space-based solar power makes the energy transition
19 work”. Some estimates suggest it could one day provide up to 80% of Europe’s renewable energy
20 needs.
21
Still, making it work is no small task. It would require enormous satellite structures,
22 complex operations and countless rocket launches. And there are cheaper renewable solutions
23 that could come online far faster — a crucial point if the world is to replace fossil fuels in time to
24 limit global warming.
25

Analyse the following statements about some grammatical structures in the text: I. The verb form “could finally make” (l. 02) expresses a future possibility. II. The sentence “The light had been collected from the Sun” (l. 07) is in the passive voice. III. The clause “whether such huge orbital structures would even be legal” (l. 34) expresses a condition. Which ones are correct?
questions.explanation: A forma modal 'could' indica possibilidade futura, e 'had been collected' é passado perfeito na voz passiva. Já 'whether' introduz uma dúvida ou pergunta indireta sobre a legalidade, não uma oração condicional.
